title: Voting systems
examples: What is the main difference between these two voting systems?
Which system makes sure smaller parties get a voice?
Can you explain how votes turn into seats in each system?

explain.say: Today we will learn about two ways to count votes. These systems decide who gets to represent people in government.
First past the post means the candidate with the most votes wins. They do not need a majority of all votes.
Proportional representation aims for seats to match vote share closely. If you get a third of votes, you get about a third of seats.
In FPTP, you vote for one person in a small local area. The person with the most votes in that area wins the seat.
In PR, your vote contributes to a party's total national vote count. This helps ensure smaller parties gain seats too.
Imagine a school election for class president. If only two people run, FPTP is clear. But if five people run, PR helps everyone feel heard.

faq.q: Does FPTP mean that the losing votes are wasted?
faq.a: People sometimes feel their vote doesn't count if their candidate doesn't win locally. Others ask if votes only count if they win, or if they are counted for the party.
asks: Does my vote matter if I don't win?

faq.q: How exactly does proportional representation calculate seats?
faq.a: It uses mathematical formulas to ensure the percentage of votes closely matches the percentage of seats. You might hear about different methods like the D'Hondt method.
asks: What is the math behind PR?
Is it just dividing votes by a number?

faq.q: Which system is better for the country?
faq.a: There is no single answer; each system has strengths and weaknesses depending on the country's goals. Some value strong single leaders, others value wide representation.
asks: Does one system always work better?

faq.q: Can a party win many votes but few seats under FPTP?
faq.a: Yes, this is possible if their votes are spread out across many different local areas. They might never have enough votes to win in any single area.
asks: Can you lose seats with many votes?
What happens if votes are spread out?

faq.q: Is proportional representation always used by big countries?
faq.a: No, many countries use variations of PR, but the specific rules change. Some smaller nations use different mix of systems.
asks: Are there different versions of PR?

facts: FPTP awards the seat to the candidate with the most votes in a single area.
PR aims for the distribution of seats to reflect the overall percentage of votes received.
PR systems often encourage smaller parties to participate in elections.
FPTP can sometimes lead to governments with a majority despite low overall support.

quiz.say: In FPTP, if Candidate A gets 30% and Candidate B gets 29% in a local area, who wins the seat?
quiz.why: Because Candidate A received the most votes in that specific local area, they win under FPTP rules.

wrong.0: This is wrong because FPTP only requires the highest vote-getter to win, not a majority.
wrong.1: This is wrong because the votes are different, so there is a clear winner based on the highest count.
wrong.3: This is wrong because Candidate B did not receive the highest number of votes in that area.

quiz.say: If a party gets 20% of the national vote using a PR system, what is their expected seat share?
quiz.why: Proportional representation tries to make the seat share match the vote share percentage as closely as possible.

wrong.0: This is wrong because PR aims for proportionality, not halving the vote share.
wrong.1: This is wrong because they only received 20% of the vote, not all of it.
wrong.2: This is wrong because PR is designed to be fair and not over-represent a party based on votes.

quiz.say: If a country uses FPTP, a party with 30% of the national vote might end up with:
quiz.why: Because FPTP focuses on local wins, a party can win many votes nationally but fail to win enough local areas for a proportional seat count.

wrong.0: This is wrong because winning more than their vote share is rare under FPTP.
wrong.1: This is wrong because they might still win some seats if their 30% is concentrated in a few areas.
wrong.3: This is wrong because that would be a perfectly proportional outcome, which FPTP does not guarantee.
